economics-001.question: Which is correct about the rule of thumb (the six-tenths rule) that the capital cost C of equipment or plants of the same type varies with capacity Q as C ∝ Q^0.6?
choices: Capital cost is proportional to capacity, so the cost per unit of capacity does not depend on scale
The larger the capacity, the higher the cost per unit of capacity
The larger the capacity, the lower the cost per unit of capacity (economies of scale)
economics-001.explanation: If C ∝ Q^0.6, the cost per unit of capacity is C/Q ∝ Q^(−0.4), which becomes smaller at larger scale. For example, doubling the capacity raises the capital cost only 2^0.6 ≈ 1.52 times, or about 0.76 times per unit of capacity. The background includes the fact that the material cost of a vessel scales with the square of its dimensions (surface area) while its capacity scales with the cube, and 0.6 is a representative exponent. Actual exponents differ by type of equipment and are used in a range of roughly 0.4–0.8. The choices saying cost is proportional (exponent 1) or rises per unit of capacity (exponent greater than 1) do not match the six-tenths rule.

economics-002.question: An existing plant with a capacity of 20 t/d cost ¥500 million to build. Using the six-tenths rule, approximately what would a plant of the same process with a capacity of 100 t/d cost (ignore price changes)?
choices: About ¥1.3 billion
¥1.5 billion
¥2.5 billion
economics-002.explanation: By the six-tenths rule, C₂ = C₁(Q₂/Q₁)^0.6. The capacity ratio is 100/20 = 5, and 5^0.6 ≈ 2.63, so C₂ ≈ ¥500 million × 2.63 ≈ ¥1.31 billion, or about ¥1.3 billion. ¥2.5 billion makes the capital cost proportional to capacity, ignoring economies of scale. ¥1.5 billion takes 5 × 0.6 = 3 times, confusing the power with multiplication. The six-tenths rule is a rough estimating method for equipment of the same process under similar conditions, and its error grows when the scale ratio is too large.

economics-003.question: The cost of building today the same unit that was built a few years ago for ¥200 million is estimated by correcting with a cost index for equipment. If the index was 500 at the time of construction and is 600 now, approximately what is the present capital cost?
choices: About ¥170 million
¥240 million
About ¥220 million
economics-003.explanation: Correction by cost index takes cost as proportional to the index: C_now = C_then × (I_now/I_then). ¥200 million × 600/500 = ¥240 million. About ¥170 million inverts the index ratio as 200 × 500/600, giving a lower estimate even though prices rose. About ¥220 million applies the six-tenths rule to the index ratio, 200 × 1.2^0.6, but the 0.6 power is a correction for differences in scale (capacity); the correction for prices is to the first power (proportional). When both scale and time differ, multiply the two corrections together.

economics-004.question: Which is correct about the Lang method, used in early-stage preliminary estimates to find the total capital cost by multiplying the total purchased cost of major equipment, such as pumps, heat exchangers and columns, by a factor?
choices: Installation and piping are already included in the equipment prices, so the total capital cost is about equal to the purchased cost and the factor is close to 1
The factor is found from the 0.6-power (six-tenths) rule according to the size of the unit, so it depends only on scale and not on the type of plant or the materials handled

Because it also covers piping, instrumentation, electrical, installation, buildings and engineering, the factor is well above 1 (often about 3–5) and varies with the materials handled (solids or fluids)
economics-004.explanation: The total capital cost of a plant includes, besides the purchase of the equipment itself, the costs of installation, piping, instrumentation, electrical work, foundations and buildings, engineering and construction management. The Lang method lumps these together and estimates them by multiplying the purchased cost of the major equipment by a factor. The factor is about 3–5 in many cases; Lang's representative values are about 3.1 for solids-processing plants and about 4.7 for fluids-processing plants, larger when fluids are handled. Its accuracy is rough, and as detailed design progresses it is replaced by equipment-specific factors or bottom-up estimates. Saying the factor is close to 1 overlooks the auxiliary costs, and the six-tenths rule is a correction for scale, distinct from this factor.

economics-005.question: Approximately what is the present value of ¥1 million to be received in 3 years, discounted at 10% per year compounded?
choices: About ¥1.33 million
economics-005.explanation: The present value of an amount F received n years from now is P = F/(1 + i)ⁿ. P = ¥1,000,000/(1.10)³ = ¥1,000,000/1.331 ≈ ¥751,000, or about ¥750,000. The two are equivalent in the sense that ¥750,000 invested today at 10% grows to ¥1 million in 3 years. ¥700,000 is the mistake of simply subtracting 30% as ¥1 million × (1 − 0.10 × 3). About ¥1.33 million is ¥1 million × 1.331, the future value in 3 years of ¥1 million today. The further in the future the amount, and the higher the discount rate, the smaller the present value.

economics-006.question: A project requires an initial investment of ¥10 million and yields a net cash income of ¥4 million at the end of each of years 1 to 3. At a discount rate of 10% per year, approximately what is the net present value (NPV) (ignore taxes and salvage value)?
choices: +¥2 million
economics-006.explanation: Discounting each year's income (in ¥ million) gives 4/1.1 + 4/1.1² + 4/1.1³ = 3.636 + 3.306 + 3.005 ≈ 9.947, and subtracting the initial investment of 10 gives NPV ≈ −0.053 (−¥53,000), or about −¥50,000. Because the NPV is slightly negative, this investment falls just short of paying off at a 10% discount rate. +¥2 million is 12 − 10 without discounting, an example where a simple total looks profitable but the conclusion changes once the time value of money is considered. About +¥910,000 discounts the three-year total of ¥12 million by only one year (1.1).

economics-007.question: Which correctly describes the internal rate of return (IRR) used to evaluate capital investments?
choices: The discount rate at which the net present value (NPV) of the investment is exactly zero
The reciprocal of the number of years to recover the initial investment
The annual profit divided by the initial investment (a simple, undiscounted return on investment)
economics-007.explanation: The internal rate of return is the discount rate at which the discounted sum of future cash flows exactly equals the initial investment, that is, the rate at which NPV = 0. It is generally found by trial and error or numerical calculation, and if the IRR exceeds the minimum rate of return the company requires (such as its cost of capital), the investment is judged profitable. For example, a project investing ¥10 million and receiving ¥4 million at the end of each year for 3 years has an NPV of about −¥50,000 at a 10% discount rate, slightly negative, and its IRR is about 9.7%, a little under 10%. The reciprocal of the payback period and the simple return on investment are different measures that ignore the time value of money and generally do not equal the IRR.

economics-008.question: Which is a correct weakness of using the simple payback period (the number of years to recover the initial investment from the annual net cash income) to evaluate a capital investment?
choices: The payback period follows from the initial investment alone, so no estimate of future cash income is needed
A project with a shorter payback period always has a larger net present value, so payback alone can rank the projects
It leaves out cash income received after the payback period and ignores the time value of money
economics-008.explanation: The simple payback period is easy to calculate and convenient for judging the safety of an investment (how quickly it pays for itself), but it does not take into account how many years the income continues after payback. As a result it can unfairly rate down a project that takes a little longer to pay back but earns for a long time. It also adds a yen from any year as having the same value, ignoring the time value of money. The discounted payback period, counted with discounted cash income, partly addresses this, but it still ignores income after payback. Even finding the payback period requires estimates of future income, and a shorter payback period does not necessarily mean a larger NPV.

economics-009.question: Two projects each require an initial investment of ¥10 million. Project A receives a single payment of ¥12 million after 1 year, and project B a single payment of ¥15 million after 5 years. When the discount rate used for evaluation is raised from 5% to 10% per year, which is correct about the change in net present value (NPV) (ignore taxes and salvage value)?
choices: The NPV of both projects is unchanged by the discount rate
The NPV of both falls, project B, whose income comes later, falls by more, and the preferred project switches from B to A
The NPV of both falls, project A, whose income comes sooner, falls by more, but B remains preferred
economics-009.explanation: NPV = F/(1 + i)ⁿ − 10 (in ¥ million). At a 5% discount rate, A = 12/1.05 − 10 ≈ +1.43 and B = 15/1.05⁵ − 10 ≈ +1.75, so B is preferred. At 10%, A = 12/1.1 − 10 ≈ +0.91 and B = 15/1.1⁵ − 10 ≈ −0.69, so only A pays off. The drop is about ¥520,000 for A and about ¥2.44 million for B. Discounting acts more strongly the larger the number of years n in (1 + i)ⁿ, so B, which depends on income in the distant future, falls by more. Because the conclusion can switch with the discount rate, it is important to check with a sensitivity analysis. The choices saying the NPV does not change or that A falls by more are wrong.

economics-010.question: Of the manufacturing costs of a chemical plant, which pair is the most appropriate example of variable costs, which rise and fall roughly in proportion to production?
choices: Depreciation and the property tax levied on equipment and land
Insurance premiums and the salaries of head-office and plant administrative staff
Raw material costs and utility costs such as steam, electricity and cooling water
economics-010.explanation: Raw materials, catalysts and chemicals, and utilities such as steam, electricity and cooling water are consumed according to how much product is made, so they are variable costs roughly proportional to production. On the other hand, depreciation, property tax, insurance, administrative salaries and much of the scheduled maintenance are fixed costs, incurred at a nearly constant level as long as the plant is owned, even if production falls. This distinction is used in break-even calculations and in estimating the cost per unit of product when the operating rate falls. Some costs, such as operator labor, can lean either way depending on how the plant is run.

economics-011.question: A product has fixed costs of ¥200 million per year, a selling price of ¥100/kg and variable costs of ¥60/kg. What is the break-even point (the annual sales volume at which profit is zero)?
choices: 5000 t/year
2000 t/year
About 3300 t/year
economics-011.explanation: For each kilogram of product, the selling price minus the variable cost, 100 − 60 = ¥40, goes toward covering fixed costs (the contribution margin). Dividing the fixed costs of ¥200 million by this gives a break-even point of 2×10⁸/40 = 5.0×10⁶ kg/year, or 5000 t/year. Selling more than this yields a profit, and selling less a loss. 2000 t/year divides the fixed costs by the selling price of ¥100, forgetting to subtract the variable cost. About 3300 t/year divides the fixed costs by the variable cost of ¥60. The higher the share of variable costs in a product, the higher its break-even point.

economics-012.question: In a plant with fixed costs, demand falls and the operating rate (production) drops. Which correctly describes the change in cost per kilogram of product (with unchanged raw material and utility consumption per unit)?
choices: Both fixed and variable costs fall in proportion to production, so neither the fixed cost nor the variable cost per kilogram changes
The variable cost per kilogram stays about the same, but the fixed costs are spread over less production, so the fixed cost per kilogram rises
Fixed costs fall with production so the fixed cost per kilogram decreases, while lower equipment efficiency raises the variable cost per kilogram
economics-012.explanation: Fixed costs are nearly constant regardless of production, so when production falls, the amount allocated to each kilogram increases. For example, fixed costs of ¥120 million per year come to ¥20/kg at 6000 t/year, but about ¥27/kg at 4500 t/year, a 75% operating rate. Variable costs are proportional to production, so with the same consumption per unit they stay about the same per kilogram. This is why, in large plants where fixed costs make up a large share, a drop in operating rate readily pushes up the cost of the product. The choice saying fixed cost per kilogram decreases thinks backwards about the amount the costs are spread over.

economics-013.question: A stirred tank operating in the turbulent regime is scaled up with geometric similarity, doubling the impeller diameter D. To keep the agitation power per unit volume P/V constant, by what factor should the rotational speed N be changed? Take the power number as constant so that P ∝ N³D⁵, and the tank volume as V ∝ D³.
choices: About 0.63 times
0.5 times
No change needed (same speed)
economics-013.explanation: Since P ∝ N³D⁵ and V ∝ D³, P/V ∝ N³D². Keeping this constant requires N³D² = constant, that is, N ∝ D^(−2/3), so doubling D gives N = 2^(−2/3) ≈ 0.63 times. 0.5 times is N ∝ 1/D, the value for keeping the impeller tip speed πND constant, a different similarity rule. Leaving the speed unchanged makes P/V 2² = 4 times larger, requiring excessive power. Constant P/V is a similarity rule often used when dispersion and mass transfer are to be kept at the same level in the larger tank.

economics-014.question: A stirred tank operating in the turbulent regime is scaled up with geometric similarity, doubling the impeller diameter D. Because the liquid is shear-sensitive, the impeller tip speed πND is kept constant. How does the agitation power per unit volume P/V compare with the original (power number constant, P ∝ N³D⁵, V ∝ D³)?
choices: It doubles
It does not change
It falls to 1/2
economics-014.explanation: Constant tip speed means N ∝ 1/D, so doubling D makes N 0.5 times. Substituting into P/V ∝ N³D² gives 0.5³ × 2² = 0.5, so P/V falls to 1/2 (the total power P is 0.5³ × 2⁵ = 4 times). Constant tip speed and constant P/V cannot both be satisfied in this way, and which one is kept changes the mixing conditions in the large tank. A lower P/V weakens dispersion and mass transfer, so when scaling up at constant tip speed, it must be checked separately whether mixing and heat transfer are adequate.

economics-015.question: A stirred tank in the turbulent regime was scaled up with geometric similarity at constant agitation power per unit volume P/V. If the product of mixing time and rotational speed, N·θm, can be taken as nearly constant in the turbulent regime, what happens to the mixing time θm in the large tank?
choices: It becomes shorter because the rotational speed increases with scale at constant P/V (about 0.6 times for a doubled impeller diameter)
It becomes longer because the rotational speed decreases (about 1.6 times for a doubled impeller diameter)
It does not change, because at the same P/V the impeller can run at the same speed as in the small tank
economics-015.explanation: At constant P/V, N ∝ D^(−2/3), so the larger the tank, the lower the rotational speed. If N·θm is constant, θm ∝ 1/N ∝ D^(2/3), so doubling the impeller diameter lengthens the mixing time 2^(2/3) ≈ 1.59 times, about 1.6 times. Even with the same P/V the mixing time cannot be preserved, and local nonuniformities in concentration or temperature tend to persist in large tanks. For this reason, when scaling up fast or strongly exothermic reactions, the feed location and feed rate are carefully designed. The choices saying the speed increases or the mixing time is unchanged are wrong.
